title: Dell R730 Quiet Fans: Supported Fixes, Raw IPMI, and a Watchdog
excerpt: What makes an R730 loud, which iDRAC8 settings actually lower fan speed, the raw IPMI override byte by byte, and a watchdog that hands control back when temperatures climb.
serp: How to quiet r730XD fans (lower idle fan speed)
R730 Noise when additional cards are plugged in.
Second PSU on R730 gets loud for a few seconds, then goes quiet

claims.claim: A typically configured R730 measures 28 dBA idle (sound pressure, LpA).
claims.quote: Idle(3): LwA-UL(4) = 4.7 bels; LpA(5)= 28 dBA; No prominent tones(6)

claims.claim: A typically configured 3.5-inch R730 measures 33 dBA operating.
claims.quote: Operating(3): LwA-UL(4) = 5.3 bels; LpA(5)= 33 dBA; No prominent tones(6)

claims.claim: A typically configured 2.5-inch R730 measures 39 dBA operating.
claims.quote: Operating(3): LwA-UL(4) = 5.8 bels; LpA(5)= 39 dBA; No prominent tones(6)

claims.claim: Dell's acoustic figures were measured at about 23 degrees C ambient.
claims.quote: Typically configured(2) 2.5” chassis in 23 ± 2 °C ambient

claims.claim: Dell measured sound pressure with the server in a 24U rack enclosure.
claims.quote: The system is placed in a 24U rack enclosure, 25 cm above reflective floor.

claims.claim: Dell's reference table equates 30 dBA with a quiet library.
claims.quote: 30 1 Quiet library

claims.claim: 65W low-power E5-2650L v3 configurations run about twice as loud as typical ones under moderate or heavy load.
claims.quote: such as an Intel Xeon E5-2650L v3 or E52630L v3 at 65W CPU, under moderate or heavy utilization, will be about twice as loud as typical configurations.

claims.claim: Low-power CPUs have lower temperature limits than standard CPUs.
claims.quote: Configurations with “low-power” CPUs (which have lower temperature limits than standard CPUs)

claims.claim: Any GPGPU card roughly doubles R730 loudness.
claims.quote: GPGPU cards: A configuration with any GPGPU card will be significantly louder (about twice as loud) than the typical configuration.

claims.claim: PCIe SSD configurations run significantly louder (table row on PCIe SSD).
claims.quote: a configuration with PCIe SSD requires more airflow for cooling and will be significantly louder than a typical configuration.

claims.claim: Performance Optimized raises fan speed and noise compared with the default DAPC profile.
claims.quote: If “Performance optimized” is selected, the fan speed/noise level will increase.

claims.claim: Dell's typical R730 configuration uses the E5-2660 v3.
claims.quote: 2 x 105W-10C CPU (Intel E5-2660 v3)

claims.claim: The R730 has N+1 fan redundancy.
claims.quote: The R730 and R730xd allow N+1 fan redundancy, allowing continuous operation with one fan failure in the system.

claims.claim: Installed hardware sets a baseline fan speed that fans do not go below unless inlet temperature or configuration changes.
claims.quote: Fan speeds may never go below this level unless the inlet ambient temperature or system configuration changes.

claims.claim: Every bay and fan slot must hold a component or a blank.
claims.quote: To ensure proper operation and cooling, all bays in the system and system fans must be populated always with either a component or with a blank.

claims.claim: Dell warns never to run the R730 without the air shroud.
claims.quote: CAUTION: Never operate your system with the air shroud removed.

claims.claim: A removed cover, shroud or blank is a listed cause of the amber temperature indicator.
claims.quote: System cover, cooling shroud, EMI filler panel, memory module blank, or back filler bracket is removed.

claims.claim: The R730 has six hot-swappable fans.
claims.quote: Your system supports six hot-swappable cooling fans.

claims.claim: The F2 System Setup path to thermal settings is iDRAC Settings > Thermal.
claims.quote: Click iDRAC Settings > Thermal .

claims.claim: The R730 BIOS System Profile defaults to Performance Per Watt Optimized (DAPC).
claims.quote: This option is set to Performance Per Watt Optimized (DAPC) by default.

claims.claim: Uncertified third-vendor hardware can run fans higher than normal or at maximum.
claims.quote: Unsupported hardware or third-vendor hardware that has not or not yet been certified might cause the system to run the fans higher than normal or even at maximum speed.

claims.claim: An uninstalled cover trips the intrusion switch and sends fans to maximum.
claims.quote: If the cover is not installed, and as a result the intrusion switch is triggered, the fan speed does increase to max as a precaution.

claims.claim: Outdated firmware can make fans run high with nothing else wrong.
claims.quote: Outdated firmware can cause fans to spin high (make noise) when nothing else is even wrong.

claims.claim: Update iDRAC, BIOS and CPLD as single updates first.
claims.quote: The first set of updates (iDRAC, BIOS, CPLD) must be done as single updates and should not be combined with any other updates.

claims.claim: Dell's fan noise article lists a damaged, missing or failed fan first among causes of high fan speed.
claims.quote: In this scenario at least one fan or fan assembly (contains two fans) is either damaged (connector, fan blade, fan blade frame), missing or failed.

claims.claim: A PowerEdge server that detects a third-party card automatically provisions extra cooling (Dell white paper, May 2015).
claims.quote: When a PowerEdge server detects a third-party card, the server automatically provisions additional cooling for the card.

claims.claim: The Dell white paper on disabling the third-party response is dated May 2015.
claims.quote: Dell Product Group | Server Engineering May 2015

claims.claim: Owner report: an R730xd idles at 43 percent fan speed.
claims.quote: Just idling in a windows install the idrac reports the fans at 43% speed (8.2Krpm)

claims.claim: Owner report: the same R730xd locks at 66 percent with a PCIe device installed.
claims.quote: If you dare add a pcie device like a quadro gpu, it is locked to 66% speed

claims.claim: Owner report: an R730xd with a ConnectX-3 ran each fan at about 17,000 rpm.
claims.quote: each of the 6 server fans runs at about 17000 RPM !!

claims.claim: Owner report: without the ConnectX-3, fans dropped to about 5,000 rpm.
claims.quote: the fans speed drops to ~5000 RPM, which seems more normal

claims.claim: Owner report: R730xd fans ran at 1 percent PWM (2,160 rpm) with Dell SSDs.
claims.quote: When the original SSDs are installed iDrac reports fans are 1% PWM / 2160 RPM.

claims.claim: Owner report: adding a non-Dell 1TB SSD raised fans to 39 to 50 percent (about 8,960 rpm).
claims.quote: As soon as i install the 1TB SSD they bump up somewhere between 39%-50% / ~8960 RPM.

claims.claim: Owner report: that owner tried disabling the third-party response via IPMI.
claims.quote: turning off hardware monitoring, or the infamous disable 3rd party monitoring via IPMI

claims.claim: Owner report: none of the attempts fixed the drive-induced ramp.
claims.quote: i DID NOT find a solution.. it's all up to Dell to release an update that allows to use third party HDD's.

claims.claim: The iDRAC8 web path to thermal settings is Overview > Hardware > Fans > Setup.
claims.quote: In the iDRAC Web interface, go to Overview > Hardware > Fans > Setup .

claims.claim: Maximum Performance thermal profile means generally higher fan speeds.
claims.quote: Generally, higher fan speeds at idle and stress loads.

claims.claim: Minimum Power thermal profile means generally lower fan speeds.
claims.quote: Generally, lower fan speeds at idle and stress loads.

claims.claim: Choosing Maximum Performance or Minimum Power overrides the BIOS System Profile's thermal settings.
claims.quote: Selecting Maximum Performance or Minimum Power , overrides thermal settings associated to System Profile setting

claims.claim: Dell recommends a reboot after a thermal profile change.
claims.quote: It is recommended to reboot the system when a thermal profile change has been made.

claims.claim: racadm ThermalProfile value 2 is Minimum Power.
claims.quote: ● 2 — Minimum Power

claims.claim: Fan Speed Offset increases fan speed over the baseline.
claims.quote: A fan speed offset causes fan speeds to increase (by the offset % value) over baseline fan speeds calculated by the Thermal Control algorithm.

claims.claim: Minimum Fan Speed is a floor; fans can run higher but not lower.
claims.quote: System fans can run higher than this speed as per thermal requirements of the system but not lower than the defined minimum speed.

claims.claim: The Maximum Exhaust Temperature Limit defaults to 70 degrees C.
claims.quote: The default value is Default, 70°C (158 °F) .

claims.claim: The exhaust limit works by changing fan speeds to keep exhaust under the limit (adding airflow).
claims.quote: This option allows the system fans speeds to change such that the exhaust temperature does not exceed the selected exhaust temperature limit.

claims.claim: A FanSpeedOffset value of 255 means no offset.
claims.quote: ● 255 — None

claims.claim: A MinimumFanSpeed reading of 255 means no user value is applied.
claims.quote: When get command reports 255, it means user configured offset is not applied.

claims.claim: Dell documents the thermal settings as persistent through reboots and iDRAC or BIOS updates.
claims.quote: they do not automatically change to the default setting during system reboot, power cycling, iDRAC, or BIOS updates.

claims.claim: A detected third-party card logs message ID PCI3018 in the Lifecycle Controller log.
claims.quote: You can confirm the presence of third-party PCI card by viewing the message ID PCI3018 in the Lifecycle Controller log.

claims.claim: Per the User's Guide, ThirdPartyPCIFanResponse 0 disables the response.
claims.quote: To disable any default fan speed response set for a detected third-party PCI card: racadm set system.thermalsettings.ThirdPartyPCIFanResponse 0

claims.claim: The RACADM CLI Guide defines ThirdPartyPCIFanResponse 0 as Disabled and 1 as Enabled.
claims.quote: ● 0 — Disabled ● 1 — Enabled Default Value Enabled

claims.claim: The 2015 white paper prints the opposite racadm value, using 1 to disable.
claims.quote: To disable the response: (default is enabled) racadm set system.thermalsettings.ThirdPartyPCIFanResponse 1

claims.claim: KB 000135682 applies to 13th generation servers including the R730 and R730xd.
claims.quote: PowerEdge R230, PowerEdge R330, PowerEdge R430, PowerEdge R530, PowerEdge R630, PowerEdge R730, PowerEdge R730xd, PowerEdge R830, PowerEdge R930

claims.claim: Status reply ending 01 00 00 means disabled; ending 00 00 00 means enabled.
The 0xce commands require an account with administrator rights.
claims.quote: Note: Ensure that the user used for any action shown above has the administrator rights needed

claims.claim: The 0xce commands can be run locally on the server or remotely over IPMI over LAN.
claims.quote: You can execute these commands either locally from the server that is being configured or remotely (IPMI over LAN)

claims.claim: Without the third-party log message, the commands have no effect on fan speed.
claims.quote: then the server isn’t treating the card as a third-party card and applying these commands will have no effect on fan speeds.

claims.claim: Disabling the response returns fans to the baseline fan speed.
claims.quote: By disabling the third-party PCIe card response, the PowerEdge thermal control system returns the fan speed to the baseline fan speed

claims.claim: Dell recommends not turning off the response without understanding the card's cooling needs.
claims.quote: It is recommended that you do not turn off the default system fan response unless you have a good understanding of the PCIe adapter cooling requirements in your system.

claims.claim: Dell's example of a safe case is a card with its own fan.
claims.quote: For example, a card that has its own cooling fan may not need additional cooling or may require less than the automatic response provides.

claims.claim: ipmitool's raw syntax is raw netfn cmd [data].
claims.quote: This will allow you to execute raw IPMI commands.

claims.claim: Network functions 30h to 3Fh are the vendor-specific (OEM) range.
claims.quote: 30h-3Fh OEM - Vendor specific (16 Network Functions)

claims.claim: 0x30 0x30 0x01 0x00 stops automatic fan adjustment regardless of temperature (community source).
claims.quote: will stop the server from adjusting fanspeed by itself, no matter the temp, letting you have full manual control

claims.claim: 0x30 0x30 0x01 0x01 returns fan control to the BIOS/iDRAC profile (community source).
claims.quote: will give back to the server the right to automate fan speed, following the profile set in bios/idrac

claims.claim: In the speed command, 0xff means every fan at once (community source).
claims.quote: Dell's speed command normally carries `0xff`, meaning "every fan at once".

claims.claim: The last byte is the fan speed percentage in hex, 0x00 to 0x64 (community source).
claims.quote: fan speed as a percentage (0-100) in hexadecimal format (0x00-0x64).

claims.claim: Local IPMI on Linux needs the OpenIPMI kernel driver.
claims.quote: IPMI management of a local system interface requires a compatible IPMI kernel driver to be installed and configured.

claims.claim: ipmitool -E reads the password from the IPMI_PASSWORD environment variable.
claims.quote: variable \fIIPMI_PASSWORD\fP or \fIIPMITOOL_PASSWORD\fP.

claims.claim: The iDRAC account used for raw fan control must be an Administrator (community source).
claims.quote: The account this container uses must be an **Administrator** on the iDRAC : fan control is not read-only

claims.claim: Owner report: 11 percent was the quietest-sounding speed on an R730.
claims.quote: In my case, with the R730 server, I found that the optimum fan speed for minimum perceived sound was 11% fan speed.

claims.claim: Owner report: lower speeds produced a more noticeable low-frequency sound.
claims.quote: I found that the lower speeds had a lower frequency sound which was actually more noticeable than the higher frequency whine at slightly higher speeds.

claims.claim: Owner report: SPX Labs tested an R330.
claims.quote: This post will cover how to silence your Dell PowerEdge R330 server.

claims.claim: Owner report: about 50 dB at idle and about 40 dB at 20 percent fan speed.
claims.quote: At idle it was about 50 decibels. After setting the fans to 20%, the server was only about 40 decibels.

claims.claim: The SPX Labs author was unsure whether the UPS was louder than the server.
claims.quote: I'm not actually sure if the server is 40 decibels or if it is my Eaton UPS making all the noise.

claims.claim: The raw commands are available on iDRAC 6, 7 and 8 (generations 11 to 13) (community source).
claims.quote: | iDRAC 6, 7 and 8 (generations 11 to 13) | Available |

claims.claim: The R710 uses iDRAC6.
claims.quote: The PowerEdge R710 Integrated Dell Remote Access Controller 6 (iDRAC6) incorporates an integrated video

claims.claim: The R720 uses iDRAC7.
claims.quote: Remote management iDRAC7 with Lifecycle Controller Express (default), iDRAC7 Enterprise (upgrade option)

claims.claim: Owner report via tigerblue77: an iDRAC6 R510 refused 0xff but accepted the command one fan at a time.
claims.quote: while accepting the very same command addressed to one fan at a time ([#378](https://github.com/tigerblue77/Dell_iDRAC_fan_controller_Docker/issues/378), on an R510)

claims.claim: sdr type temperature lines end in a reading such as 28 degrees C.
claims.quote: Baseboard Temp   | 30h | ok  |  7.1 | 28 degrees C

claims.claim: Unreadable sensors are listed as No Reading instead of a temperature (community source).
claims.quote: a socket that is empty or unreadable is usually still listed, but as `Disabled` or `No Reading` instead of a temperature

claims.claim: Manual mode returns to automatic on an iDRAC reset (community source).
claims.quote: It will return to automatic mode upon an iDRAC reset.

claims.claim: Intel lists a Tcase of 79 degrees C for the E5-2660 v3.
claims.quote: TCASE 79°C

claims.claim: tigerblue77 suggests a threshold slightly below Tcase (community source).
claims.quote: Check `Tcase` (case temperature) of your CPU on Intel Ark website and then set `CPU_TEMPERATURE_THRESHOLD` to a slightly lower value.

claims.claim: Hess advises testing under synthetic loads before trusting a static speed.
claims.quote: However, it is worth double-checking your temperatures and running some synthetic loads to see what the worse case would look like.

claims.claim: The tigerblue77 container applies Dell's default profile when it stops.
claims.quote: applies Dell's default dynamic fan control profile, handing the fans back to the iDRAC;

claims.claim: Community reports: iDRAC9 accepts the raw commands up to 3.30.30.30.
claims.quote: | iDRAC 9 up to firmware `3.30.30.30` | Available, that being the newest version they are confirmed to work on |

claims.claim: Community reports: iDRAC9 refuses the raw commands from 3.34.34.34.
claims.quote: | iDRAC 9 from firmware `3.34.34.34` on | **Removed by Dell**, deliberately and for good |

claims.claim: Behavior on 3.31 and 3.32 is unreported.
claims.quote: `3.31.31.31` and `3.32.32.32` sit between those two versions and what either answers has never been reported.

claims.claim: Owner report: a T440 on iDRAC9 3.34.34.34 got Insufficient privilege level.
claims.quote: Unable to send RAW command (channel=0x0 netfn=0x30 lun=0x0 cmd=0x30 rsp=0xd4): Insufficient privilege level

claims.claim: A Dell representative said access would not be allowed going forward.
claims.quote: Going forward access is not going to be allowed as it affects the thermal algorithms and cooling the system.

claims.claim: After the June 2024 release, iDRAC9 cannot be downgraded to 4.40.10.00 or older.
claims.quote: iDRAC9 firmware 4.40.10.00 or older after updating to the June 2024 iDRAC9 firmware release.

claims.claim: The June 2024 release is 7.00.00.172 on 14th generation servers.
Sound Cap caps CPU power to limit fan speed, reducing performance.
claims.quote: System sets cap to CPU power to limit fan speed, consequently limiting acoustics. System performance is expected to be reduced as a result.

claims.claim: Some platforms do not support some custom cooling options.
claims.quote: Some Dell EMC server platforms may not support some or any of these custom cooling options.

claims.claim: On iDRAC9 the third-party response is changed slot by slot.
claims.quote: Note that Dell EMC only allows third-party PCIe adapter default cooling responses to be disabled or customized on a slot-by-slot basis.

claims.claim: There is no customer-facing IPMI support for the third-party response on iDRAC9.
claims.quote: There is no customer-facing support for configuring the third-party PCIe fan response through IPMI.

claims.claim: Per-slot racadm command to disable the response on iDRAC9.
claims.quote: racadm set system.pcieslotlfm.1.lfmmode disabled

claims.claim: LFMMode defaults to Automatic.
claims.quote: DefaultValue = Automatic

claims.claim: The server does not allow fan speeds below the threshold it needs.
claims.quote: the server does not allow fan speeds to drop below the threshold that is required to cool the server and any adapters that Dell provides.

claims.claim: Owner report: replacement Noctua fans did not exceed 1600 rpm.
claims.quote: the noctua's are pwm controlled the same way as the oem fans and didnt push past 1600rpm

claims.claim: Owner report: the Noctua fans were half the depth of the stock fans.
claims.quote: same size dimensions so they fit in the fan space but half the depth.

claims.claim: Owner report: the Dell plugs were cut off and soldered to the Noctua wiring.
claims.quote: Cut the plugs off of the fan housing and then solder them to the noctua wiring.

claims.claim: Owner report: no heat issues with a Quadro P2000 installed.
claims.quote: 1x P2000 Quadro card, 1x 4 port usb card, 2x CPU's, 198gb of memory. No heat issues atall and a fraction of the noise!

claims.claim: Owner report: an R710 logged a fan below the lower critical threshold.
claims.quote: Fan 1 RPM is operating less than the lower critical threshold.

claims.claim: Owner report: in that state all fans spun around 12,000 rpm.
claims.quote: all fans + PSU fan start spinning around 12k RPM.

claims.claim: ipmitool sensor list shows sensor thresholds.
claims.quote: Lists sensors and thresholds in a wide table format.

claims.claim: A SIGKILLed controller leaves fans at the static speed with nothing to raise them (community source).
claims.quote: Past that timeout the container is `SIGKILL`ed, which no program can catch or delay, and **the fans stay at your `FAN_SPEED` with nothing left to raise them**.

claims.claim: Owner report: manual mode stuck through several reboots.
claims.quote: I ran the commands once and they stuck, even after a few reboots.

claims.claim: Owner report: manual mode sometimes does not survive an iDRAC power off or reboot.
claims.quote: Note: This sometimes does sometimes not survive an idrac power off or system reboot.

claims.claim: Any iDRAC reset, including a firmware update, restores automatic mode (community source).
claims.quote: This can happen if the iDRAC is reset in any way (FW update, SW reset, sustained power outage).

claims.claim: A non-Administrator account gets the same completion code (0xd4) as firmware without the commands (community source).
claims.quote: a lesser account is refused it with the very completion code (`0xd4`) a firmware that removed the commands returns.

claims.claim: ipmitool prints completion code 0xd4 as Insufficient privilege level.
claims.quote: { 0xd4, "Insufficient privilege level" },

claims.claim: Remote IPMI commands need IPMI over LAN configured.
claims.quote: If IPMI over LAN is not configured, then external systems cannot communicate with the iDRAC server using IPMI commands.

claims.claim: racadm command to enable IPMI over LAN.
claims.quote: racadm set iDRAC.IPMILan.Enable 1

claims.claim: CISA warns attackers can easily find and access Internet-connected IPMI systems.
claims.quote: Attackers can easily identify and access systems that run IPMI and are connected to the Internet.

claims.claim: Disabling the response on passive cards can cause NIC and disk problems (community source).
claims.quote: Strange behavior includes but is not limited to: packet loss on nics, loss of tcp states, hdd disconnects and smart errors, etc.

photos.why: A PowerEdge R720xd at Dell Enterprise Innovation Day (May 17, 2016), the 12th generation sibling behind the 'dell r720 quiet fans' variant. Commons has no R730 photo.
